headline: Elevation requires sustained effort against gravity—but height provides perspective and advantage
universal_truth: Going up is hard; that's why high ground is valuable; the effort creates the advantage
fun_facts: Climbing stairs burns about 0.17 calories per step—going up requires 5x more energy than walking on flat ground
Mount Everest's summit has only 33% of sea-level oxygen—height has costs as well as benefits
The world's longest escalator is 453 feet—we build tools to make elevation easier
discussion_questions: Where in your life are you trying to 'go up'?
What's the view from the heights you've achieved?
When is the climb worth the effort?

hook.script: Climbing stairs leaves you winded. Climbing mountains leaves you exhausted. Going up fights gravity—it costs energy. But height provides advantage: better view, strategic position, achievement. The effort creates the value.

cliff.script: We use 'up' metaphorically: rising to challenges, climbing the ladder, reaching the top. Why is elevation so central to how we think about achievement?
cliff.prompt: Why do we associate up with better?

options.text: Height provides real advantages—better view, strategic position, harder for others to reach—and the effort required creates scarcity, making heights valuable
options.response: Yes. High ground is valuable precisely because it's hard to reach. The effort filters out those who won't pay the cost. Difficulty is part of the value.

options.text: It's just a metaphor—up has no real advantage
options.response: It's metaphorical, but rooted in real physics—height does provide advantages...

fact1.title: Fighting Gravity
fact1.script: Going up means working against Earth's gravity. Every foot of elevation requires lifting your weight that distance. It's never free. This is why elevation costs energy—it's physics, not weakness.

fact2.title: Height Advantages
fact2.script: Height provides perspective—you see more from above. It provides safety—threats are below. It provides achievement—others can see you've climbed. These advantages justify the cost.

fact3.title: Sustainable Ascent
fact3.script: You can't sprint up a mountain—sustainable climbing requires pacing. The same in life: rapid rises exhaust you. Steady climbing, with rest, reaches higher than burst-and-crash approaches.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Going up is hard—that's why high ground is valuable. The effort creates the advantage. Climb steadily, climb sustainably.

outro.script: That's Day 230! Tomorrow, we'll explore making structures—engineering. Until then, assess where you're climbing and whether your pace is sustainable.

growTrack.title: Climb Assessment - Where Are You Going Up?
growTrack.activity: Where in your life are you 'climbing'—working toward elevation? Is the pace sustainable? What's the view from where you are now? Sometimes pausing to appreciate progress gives energy for the next stage of the climb.
